source.title: BDS-Adam optimizer integrating adaptive variance rectification with semi-adaptive gradient smoothing
source.authors: Yichuan Shao; Shiqian Weng; Haijing Sun; Qian Gao; Le Zhang; Zhiqiang Mao; Shuai Xu; Zhi-Tao Zhang; Lei Xing

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The paper contains some internal inconsistencies in dataset descriptions and reported results, noted below.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares Adam with SGD on three image datasets and reports Adam with higher test accuracy in each, refining the adaptive-optimizer comparison in V4. It does not measure the train–test gap.
record.gate_note: The paper reports optimizer test accuracy and loss, but no train error, random-label fitting, or train–test gap. It also reports optimizer ablations and smoothing-coefficient comparisons; these do not test the mapped claim versions. The V4 comparison uses a fixed shared learning rate, not a systematic comparison under limited tuning.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out image classification performance. Adam outperforms SGD at the shared learning rate, qualifying V4's scope. Training performance is unnecessary to test the held-out-performance comparison, although its relationship to training performance remains untested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that BDS-Adam improves classification accuracy, convergence, and stability over Adam and other baselines across the tested image datasets. They acknowledge additional tuning requirements and untested applicability beyond these domains. Their superiority claims are not uniform across every individual loss comparison.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares optimizers using its own image-classification setup and fixed shared learning rates; it does not reproduce Wilson et al.'s broader benchmark or tuning protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and learning-rate setting; the paper also reports optimizer performance at 0.0001 on CIFAR-10, but that comparison does not isolate adaptive optimizers versus SGD for the mapped claim.
record.problems: No train accuracy or train error is reported, so the train–test gap cannot be assessed. The three single-run comparison tables give no uncertainty estimates. The paper's dataset description is inconsistent: Stomach is described as 1,885 images in the setup and 3,200 in a later passage; the reported table and text also differ on some Stomach and CIFAR-10 values.
record.rows_left_out: Test-loss comparisons against SGD were not extracted as additional rows because the mapped V4 claim concerns held-out performance relative to training performance, and training performance is absent. Results in Tables 7–8 aggregate five runs and compare multiple baselines with BDS-Adam rather than testing the mapped Adam-versus-SGD claim.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.

Separate learning-rate and schedule tuning for SGD and adaptive baselines; equal or better training performance; broader tuning; controlled weight-decay or optimizer-switching interventions; language benchmarks.
Batch-size effects and changes to the training recipe that compensate for large batches.
Controlled dropout comparisons, including interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Identification and removal of memorized training examples followed by retraining.

missing.what: Standard adaptive-baseline comparisons with SGD: MNIST Adagrad 98.00%, AdamW 98.56%, and NAdam 98.59% versus SGD 97.55%; CIFAR-10 50.05%, 78.84%, and 57.65% versus 41.23%; Stomach 69.80%, 76.20%, and 76.80% versus 72.60%. Adagrad on Stomach supplies a supporting condition absent from the extracted rows.

record.verdict_notes: V4 says adaptive methods often perform worse, so reversed results under one shared learning rate qualify its scope rather than overturning it. The five-run results in Tables 7–8 were explicitly declared omitted and therefore are not listed as missing, but their exclusion rationale is incorrect: their baseline values also bear on V4. CIFAR-10 mean accuracy favors Adam over SGD, 78.03±0.48% versus 56.62±1.23%; Stomach means are close, 66.40±1.55% versus 66.04±2.02%. Table 8 reverses the single-comparison Stomach loss ordering: Adam 1.2042 versus SGD 0.9862. Reported significance tests compare baselines with BDS-Adam, not Adam with SGD. Code availability is stated as wengshiqian/BDS-Adam.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Training performance, broader tuning, language benchmarks, weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and word-level language models.
Batch-size comparisons and fixed-epoch large-batch effects.
Dropout effects and interaction with weight decay or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

relationships.condition: Adam versus SGD at shared learning rate 0.001, batch size 128, and 100 epochs on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Stomach
relationships.reason: R1–R6 show higher Adam accuracy on all three datasets: 98.61 versus 97.55%, 78.04 versus 41.23%, and 76.40 versus 72.60%. These are exceptions under fixed settings; separately tuned SGD was not tested.
relationships.display_finding: Reported Adam accuracy advantages across all three datasets remain unverified and do not compare separately tuned optimizers.

relationships.display_finding: Reported accuracy was lower and reported loss higher for Adagrad than SGD, but the comparison remains unverified.
